title: Slice a big hailstone in half and you find rings inside, like an onion
body: A hailstone starts as a tiny frozen droplet inside a thunderstorm, carried upward by winds that can blow at up to **180 km/h**. As it moves through the cloud it keeps collecting ice. Where it passes through lots of supercooled water droplets it gains a layer of clear ice; where there is mostly water vapour, it gains a layer of cloudy white ice. A strong updraft can hold it aloft for at least 30 minutes, so a large stone can build up many alternating shells.

cover.alt: A huge lumpy white hailstone lying on a towel next to a tape measure that shows it is about 20 cm across

slides.question: How wide was the largest hailstone ever officially measured?
slides.explanation: About 20 cm across, with a circumference of 47.3 cm. It fell on Vivian, South Dakota, on 23 July 2010, and it is the stone on the cover.

slides.label: the heaviest hailstone on record
slides.text: It fell in Gopalganj District, Bangladesh, on 14 April 1986.

slides.alt: A hailstone cut in half on a wooden board, showing rings of clear and milky white ice around a white core
slides.caption: A hailstone cut open. Each ring is a layer of ice it picked up on its way through the storm cloud.

slides.heading: How fast hailstones fall
slides.note: Estimates: real speeds vary with shape, wind, collisions and melting

slides.question: What gives a growing hailstone a layer of clear ice?
slides.explanation: Water droplets freeze onto the stone as clear ice. Where there is mostly water vapour instead, the new layer is opaque and white.
